extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics / mathematical physics (pendula, fluid statics and resistance laws)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of classical-mechanics propositions (theorems/problems) concerning fluid density under gravity, laws of mutual particle forces, and pendulum oscillations with various resistance laws (time-proportional, velocity-proportional, quadratic, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXII. THEOREMA XVII
rubrics_metrics.description: If the compressive force (vis compressiva) is proportional to density and the gravities of the fluid particles are reciprocally proportional to the squares of their distances from a center, and distances are taken in geometric progression, then the densities of the fluid at those distances are in geometric progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct perpendicular ordinates at points whose abscissas are in geometric progression; the differences of densities correspond to ordinates cut from a hyperbola whose asymptotes relate to the geometric progression. In the infinitesimal limit the sum of differences corresponds to hyperbolic area; thus one can recover an intermediate density by comparing appropriate hyperbolic areas. Corollary and scholium: variants arise if gravity decreases in other power-laws (inverse-cube, inverse-fourth, etc.) or if compression-law links density to compressive force with different exponents — the same method gives corresponding progression laws for density when distances are taken in arithmetic/geometric progressions accordingly. Practical note: for Earth's atmosphere, density is (approximately) proportional to compressive force, consistent with barometer observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium to Prop. XXII (generalizations on gravity and compression laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations: if gravity of fluid particles diminishes in inverse-cube, inverse-fourth, etc., of distance and certain sequences of distances (arithmetical, etc.) are taken, then resulting densities form geometric progressions under analogous constructions; conversely, different compression-laws (e.g., compressive force proportional to some power of density) yield different power-relations between density and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if gravitas diminishes in triplicate (inverse-cube) ratio of distance, and cubes of distances are summed in arithmetic progression, then densities are geometric; if compressive force is proportional to square of density (or other power-laws), combine with gravity power-law to deduce density ∝ distance^{-n/(m)} for appropriate exponents. The scholium emphasizes these are mathematical possibilities; experiments indicate air density is (nearly) proportional to compressive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXIII. THEOREMA XVIII
rubrics_metrics.description: If a fluid is composed of mutually repelling particles whose density is proportional to compression, then the centrifugal (repulsive) forces of the particles are reciprocally proportional to the distances of their centers; conversely, particles whose mutual forces are reciprocally proportional to distances will form an elastic fluid whose density is proportional to compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses two similar cubic volumes (before and after compression) and compares pressures exerted by corresponding plane elements; deduces that the forces sustaining these pressures (centrifugal forces) scale reciprocally with interparticle distances. The converse is shown by reversing the proportionality chain: forces ↔ pressures ↔ densities ↔ compressing force. This proposition links microscopic interparticle force laws to macroscopic elastic response (density vs. compression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium to Prop. XXIII (powers generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If centrifugal forces vary inversely as higher powers of distance (duplicate, triplicate, etc.), the resulting relations between cubes (or other powers) of compressing forces and powers of density follow accordingly; in general if forces ∝ distance^{-n}, then compressing forces scale with density to index (n+2) and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives algebraic pattern: denote distance by D and density by E; if centrifugal forces ∝ D^{-n}, then compressing forces ∝ E^{(n+2)/?} (text gives index relations). Note the statements apply to forces that terminate locally (short-range interactions); infinite-range propagation of particle forces would change macroscopic behavior (requires larger forces to achieve same compression). Examples: magnetic attraction is largely local via intervening laminas.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXIV. THEOREMA XIX
rubrics_metrics.description: For pendula whose centers of oscillation are equally distant from the suspension point, the quantities of matter (masses) in the bodies are in the ratio composed of the ratio of their weights and the duplicate ratio (square) of their oscillation times in vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: velocity generated by a given force in a given mass over time is ∝ force × time / mass. For equal length pendula, driving forces ∝ weights; arc subdivisions produce proportional velocities and times. Conclude mass ∝ weight × (time)^2 / (other factors) — corollaries: if times equal then masses ∝ weights; if weights equal then masses ∝ square of times; if masses equal then weights ∝ inverse square of times; overall mass of a pendulum ∝ weight × (time)^2 × (pendulum length)^{-1}. Corol.6 notes distinction between absolute weight in vacuum and comparative weight in a resisting medium; experimental remark: experiments confirm mass proportional to weight for bodies examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXV. THEOREMA XX
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendula in a medium where resistance is proportional to moments of time, and pendula of the same specific gravity in a non-resistant medium, execute oscillations in the cycloid in the same time and their corresponding arcs are described proportionally (isochronism under time-proportional resistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: represent accelerating force at a point by arc-length of the cycloid; represent resistance (time-proportional) by another given arc; show that at every stage the driving forces, velocities, and remaining arcs scale so that two pendula (one with time-proportional resistance, one without resistance) traverse proportional arcs synchronously and complete full oscillations in equal times. Corollary: maximum speed in the resisting medium does not occur at the cycloid bottom C but at a different point O where the cycloid arc is bisected; ascent/descent retardations are symmetric in stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXVI. THEOREMA XXI
rubrics_metrics.description: If pendula experience resistance proportional to velocities, then oscillations in a cycloid are isochronous (same period) — i.e., cycloidal pendulum remains isochronous even under velocity-proportional resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if velocities in corresponding arc-parts are proportional to total arcs, then resistances (being proportional to velocities) are also proportional to those arcs; subtracting/adding the resistances to the gravitational driving forces preserves proportionality of increments/decrements of velocities so that velocities remain proportional to full arcs at all times. Initial conditions yield the proportionality, hence the pendula describe corresponding arcs simultaneously and periods coincide. (This is a general proof of isochronism under linear resistance laws for cycloidal motion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXVII. THEOREMA XXII
rubrics_metrics.description: If pendula experience resistance proportional to the square (duplicate ratio) of velocities, then the differences between oscillation times in the resisting medium and the times in the same-gravity non-resisting medium are (approximately) proportional to the arcs described while oscillating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For equal pendula describing unequal arcs: resistance in an arc is (approximately) proportional to square of velocity, i.e., proportional to square of the arc (AA : BB :: resistance). If resistances scale as squares of arcs, the excess time due to resistance in each arc is proportional to the corresponding arc; hence differences of times in resistant medium versus vacuum are proportional to the arcs described. Corollaries: from measured times in a resisting medium one can infer vacuum oscillation times; shorter oscillations are more nearly isochronous and are executed in nearly the same time as in vacuum; longer arcs have slightly larger periods due to asymmetric resistive effects in descent vs ascent. Practical note: medium motion affects small corrections: accelerating bodies experience slightly different effective resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXVIII. THEOREMA XXIII
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pendulum oscillating in a cycloid experiences resistance proportional to moments of time, then the ratio of its resistance to the gravitational force equals the excess of the descent arc over the subsequent ascent arc divided by twice the pendulum length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate BC the arc of descent and Ca the arc of ascent; their difference A a relates to resistive force. Using constructions from Prop. XXV, represent driving and resisting forces by cycloid arcs; the ratio resistance/gravity = (excess descent arc)/(2 × pendulum length). This gives an apparatus to determine resistive force from measured discrepancy between descent and ascent arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXIX. PROBLEMA VI
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a pendulum in a cycloid with resistance proportional to the square of the velocity, find the resistance at each point along the arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution: long geometric construction using a straight line cut into points and a hyperbola whose areas correspond to cycloid arcs and driving forces; by selecting perpendiculars that cut hyperbolic areas proportional to particular cycloid arcs one can construct areas Y and Z whose difference gives the area that represents the resistance R at point D. Conclusion: the resistance at point D relative to gravity is as a constructed hyperbolic-area difference to another hyperbolic area representing the gravitational driving force. Corollaries: one can deduce the extremal and infimum values and infer local velocities from the obtained resistances (velocity ∝ inverse subduplicate ratio of resistance). The proposition remarks the algebra is difficult and motivates the subsequent proposition which gives simpler constructions/approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXX. THEOREMA XXIV
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line AB equal to the cycloid arc is drawn and at each point D erect a perpendicular DK whose length is to the pendulum length as the resistance at the corresponding arc-point is to gravity, then the difference between total descent arc and total subsequent ascent arc, multiplied by the semisum of those arcs, equals the area occupied by all such perpendiculars (area BKT a? in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition: represent accelerative and resistive effects by lengths along AB and by the perpendiculars DK; consider infinitesimal motions and triangles to relate velocity decrements caused by resistance to increments produced by gravity; sum/integrate to equate the total area under the perpendicluars to the integrated arc-difference expression. Corollaries and approximations: (1) uniform resistance => the figure under perpendiculars is a rectangle and gives direct proportional relations; (2) resistance ∝ velocity => the figure is approximately an ellipse and gives relation resistance/gravity ∝ Aa / pendulum_length (with numerical constants noted); (3) resistance ∝ velocity^2 => the figure approximates a parabola and corresponding proportionalities follow. Practical note: these approximations are judged sufficiently accurate for practical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXXI. THEOREMA XXV
rubrics_metrics.description: If the resistances acting on an oscillating body in each small part of its described arcs are increased or decreased in a given ratio, then the difference between the descent arc described and the subsequent ascent arc increases or decreases in the same given ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the arc-difference arises from the total retardation of the pendulum due to resistance, so any proportional scaling of the local resistances scales the total retardation and hence the arc-difference by the same factor. Corollaries: (1) if resistance ∝ velocity then the arc-difference scales like the total arc described; (2) if resistance ∝ velocity^2 then the arc-difference scales like the square (duplicate ratio) of the total arc; (3) for any power-law or mixed law (partly linear, partly quadratic) the arc-difference decomposes into components following the same mixture of power-ratios; (4) from successive unequal arcs one can infer the ratio of increment/decrement of the arc-difference and thereby determine how resistive components vary with velocity (practical method for experimentally inferring resistive law).
